## The same interval twice, and you won't recognise it twice

Play two notes one after the other and you hear motion: a direction, a distance,
an arrival. Strike the same two notes together and the motion vanishes. What's
left is a colour, built out of fusion, beating and roughness. Learning one
presentation buys you surprisingly little of the other, so keep two descriptions
per interval and expect them to disagree.

Your own words work better than borrowed ones, provided they point at something
you hear every time. "Small and tense." "Open, almost hollow." Keep each phrase
tied to the register, the direction and the synth that produced it until you
find out how much of it travels.

## Four distances, played two ways each

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 68
use_synth :piano

intervals = {1 => "minor second", 4 => "major third", 7 => "perfect fifth", 12 => "octave"}
root = note(:c4)

intervals.each do |distance, label|
  play root, release: 0.7
  sleep 1
  play root + distance, release: 0.7
  sleep 2

  play root, release: 2
  play root + distance, release: 2
  sleep 3
  puts "#{distance} semitones: #{label}"
end
```

Follow the leap on the first pass. On the second, stop following anything and
listen to the blend. The label arrives after both, which leaves you a few beats
to commit to a description before the name overwrites it. Say yours out loud
before the log prints, and notice which of the four you reached for fastest.

## Change what varies

1. Reverse the melodic pairs and leave the harmonic ones alone. Does a
   descending minor second still feel tense to you, or does it feel like relief?
2. Restore the ascending forms and move `root` to `note(:fs3)`. Distances are
   untouched, register isn't. Mark which of your descriptions survive the move.
3. Restore C4, then play the harmonic pairs through `:sine` while the melodic
   pairs keep `:piano`. Sine tones expose beating and fusion; the piano's attack
   makes two separate events easy to locate. Don't compare smoothness across
   that change without writing the timbre down.

## Build the dictionary out of contrasts

Four distances, chosen because they don't resemble each other, teach you more
than twelve copied from someone else's list. A minor second gets sharper next to
a major third. A fifth defines itself against an octave. While you're still
building the associations, show the label right after the sound so the two
arrive together; shuffle the order later, when the question changes from "what
does this sound like" to "can you retrieve the name."

Change the root only after all four have descriptions that hold up. If every
major third you've ever heard is C4 to E4, you've learned a pair of pitches and
not a relation. Transposition is the test for that.

Tune anchors are worth having and worth auditing. A remembered song often starts
on a pickup, decorates the target, or sits between two degrees you've
misremembered. Store the exact two notes and the direction. When an anchor keeps
producing wrong answers, delete it.

[Lesson 20](20-build-your-own-drill-harness.qmd) turns this reference material into a drill: prompt, pause, reveal.

## Start with four rows

Build a hash whose keys run from 0 to 12 semitones. Every completed row holds
the standard label, an ascending description, a descending description, a
harmonic description, and a tune anchor if you have an honest one.

Fill four rows, audition all their presentations in Sonic Pi 5, and rewrite any
description that doesn't point at a repeatable cue. Then test yourself in mixed
order. Add a fifth interval only after two consecutive sessions of nine correct
out of ten. Four rows backed by evidence beat twelve rows of inherited
adjectives.
